The full answer for this step, with every rule and source
My ex wants to change our final order — what do I have to do, and by when?

Where things stand

Another party has served you with a motion to change a final order or agreement. The rules give you two ways to reply. Which one you use depends on whether you agree to the change. Your time to reply depends on where you live.

What to do next

Do you disagree with the change, or want the court to make an added or different change? Then you must serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B), with all required attachments. You must do this within 30 days after you get the motion to change and its papers, if you live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, the limit is 60 days. Do you agree to the change, or have you and the other party agreed to a different change? Then you must fill in the parts of the consent motion to change (Form 15C) that apply to you. Within the same 30 or 60 days, you must return a signed copy to the party making the motion. You must also give a copy of the signed consent to the assignee, if there is one. An assignee is an agency or person a support order or agreement has been assigned to. If the order or agreement was assigned, you must serve your response on the assignee as if it were a party. You may use an affidavit to give the facts that support your side. It can replace Parts C and D of Form 15B, or add to them. Rules 14 (18) and (19) apply to that affidavit. Does the motion ask to change a final support order or a support agreement? Then you must serve and file a financial statement within the same time as your response or consent. Your response (Form 15B) must be served and filed at the same time as the financial statement. This is subject to rule 13 (1.3). Under it, a party making a claim does not have to file a financial statement in one case. That is when their only support claim is for child support in the table amount. That does not apply if there is also a property claim. It also does not apply if there is a claim for exclusive possession (sole use) of the matrimonial home and its contents. The motion may not need a financial statement, but your response may ask to change a support order or support agreement. If so, the financial statement rules apply to you too. With a financial statement, you must serve other papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They include the papers in rule 13 (3.1) and a current list of what is owed from the Family Responsibility Office. If you are the one asking to change or cancel arrears, you must also serve proof of your income for each of those years. This is your income tax return with your notice of assessment, and any notice of reassessment. If those notices are unavailable for a year, use the Canada Revenue Agency's Income and Deductions printout with the return instead. If you do not have to file a tax return and chose not to because of the Indian Act (Canada), serve some other proof of income. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with those papers. File the certificate no later than four days before a case conference. Your response may make a claim about decision-making responsibility or parenting time, net family property, a matrimonial home, or support. If it does, the clerk may give you an automatic order (Form 8.0.1). If the clerk gives you one, you must serve it on every other party. Serve it promptly, and no later than seven days after it is issued.

Your deadline

If you do not agree, or want the court to make an added or different change, serve and file a response (Form 15B). If you agree, return a signed consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion. Give a copy to any assignee. You have 30 days after the day you receive the motion to change and its supporting documents. It is 60 days if you do not live in Canada or the United States. The motion may ask to change support, or your response may ask for a support change. If so, your financial statement is due in the same time. Serve the papers the rule lists with it. Examples are the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) and a current schedule of arrears from the Family Responsibility Office. Add a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). Your response may ask for its own change to parenting, property or support. If the clerk then issues an automatic order, serve it promptly, and no later than 7 days after it is issued. Where the information program applies, your certificate must be filed before you serve the response. This is explained below. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take any step in the case except booking a case conference. The rule's other exception is for an answer. It does not mention a response to a motion to change. So where the program applies, attend it and file your certificate before your response is due. Or ask the court on a motion to excuse you. The rule counts the 45 days from when the case started. It says nothing more exact for a motion to change.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

Based on the date you gave us, the last day for this is Monday 2 November 2026.

How that was counted:
- Counted 30 days from Friday 2 October 2026, not counting that day itself and counting the last day, which gives Sunday 1 November 2026.
- Sunday 1 November 2026 is a Sunday, when court offices are closed.
- The period therefore ends on the next day court offices are open: Monday 2 November 2026.

This date was worked out by counting, not taken from your court file. If the date you gave us is not exactly right, this one will not be either — and the court office can confirm both.

What happens after

Say you do not serve and file a response, or return a consent, as required. Then these things apply, unless a court orders otherwise. You do not get notice of more steps in the case, except service of an order. You cannot take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without you, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. The party making the motion may also file a motion form (Form 14B) asking the court to make the order they asked for in their papers. They cannot do this if an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest and opposes the change. If the motion is opposed, a judge must hold at least one conference. Even after you serve and file a response, the parties and any assignee may still agree before the hearing. They may then go ahead on consent by filing the papers rule 15 (19) lists.

“Before the court makes a variation order in respect of a child support order, the court shall satisfy itself that a change of circumstances as provided for in the applicable guidelines has occurred since the making of the child support order or the last variation order made in respect of that order.”

Marginal note: Conditions of order (3) The court may include in a variation order any provision that under this Act could have been included in the order in respect of which the variation order is sought, and the court has the same powers and obligations that it would have when making that order. Affidavit based on personal knowledge (18) An affidavit for use on a motion shall, as much as possible, contain only information within the personal knowledge of the person signing the affidavit. O. Reg. 114/99, r. 14 (18). Affidavit based on other information (19) The affidavit may also contain information that the person learned from someone else, but only if, (a) the source of the information is identified by name and the affidavit states that the person signing it believes the information is true; and (b) in addition, if the motion is a contempt motion under rule 31, the information is not likely to be disputed. O. Reg. 114/99, r. 14 (19). Restrictions on evidence (20) The following restrictions apply to evidence for use on a motion, unless the court orders otherwise: 1. The party making the motion shall serve all the evidence in support of the motion with the notice of motion. 2. The party responding to the motion shall then serve all the evidence in response. 3. The party making the motion may then serve evidence replying to any new matters raised by the evidence served by the party responding to the motion. 4. No other evidence may be used. O. Reg. 114/99, r. 14 (20).

Request for order (15) If a party does not serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B) or return a consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion as required under subrule (9), or if the party’s response is struck out by an order, the party making the motion to change may file a motion form (Form 14B) asking that the court make the order requested in the materials filed by the party, unless an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest in the motion and opposes the change. O. Reg. 151/08, s. 4; O. Reg. 322/13, s. 9 (2). Consent to motion (16) If a party returns to the party making the motion a consent motion to change (Form 15C) in accordance with subparagraph 2 i of subrule (9), the party making the motion shall complete and file the consent motion to change and, unless any assignee refuses to consent to the change being requested, the party making the motion shall file with the consent motion to change, (a) a motion form (Form 14B) asking that the court make the order described in the consent motion to change; (b) five copies of a draft order; (c) a stamped envelope addressed to each party and to the assignee, if any; and (d) if the order that is agreed on relates in whole or in part to a support obligation, (i) a support deduction order information form prescribed under the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, and (ii) a draft support deduction order. O. Reg. 151/08, s. 4.

Support if family violence is part of your situation
Who to contact, and how

If family violence is part of what you're dealing with, Ontario has support services separate from the court process itself. A Family Court Support Worker can help you understand and go through the family court process if you're a victim of domestic violence -- Family Court Support Workers do not give legal advice, but they can help you understand what's happening and connect you to other services. Every courthouse also has a Family Law Information Centre (FLIC) that provides information about the court process and referrals to local resources.

Ontario also names specific support organizations for family violence:
- Assaulted Women's Helpline: 1-866-863-0511 (toll-free), or 416-863-0511
- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- Victim Support Line: 1-888-579-2888 (toll-free), or 416-314-2447

The Family Court Support Worker Program and the Family Law Information Centre are delivered locally through each court location rather than through a single province-wide phone number. To find the Family Court Support Worker for your court, use Ontario's own listing of service providers by court location, which links directly to the organization delivering the program there. To reach the Family Law Information Centre, contact or visit the courthouse handling your case -- Ontario's own courthouse listing gives the address and contact information, including a phone number, for each location.

Attend the mandatory information program. 45 days after the day the case was started. Give the date below and we will count the last day for you.

Do you disagree with the change, or want the court to make an added or different change? Then you must serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B), with all required attachments. You must do this within 30 days after you get the motion to change and its papers, if you live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, the limit is 60 days. Do you agree to the change, or have you and the other party agreed to a different change? Then you must fill in the parts of the consent motion to change (Form 15C) that apply to you. Within the same 30 or 60 days, you must return a signed copy to the party making the motion. You must also give a copy of the signed consent to the assignee, if there is one. An assignee is an agency or person a support order or agreement has been assigned to. If the order or agreement was assigned, you must serve your response on the assignee as if it were a party. You may use an affidavit to give the facts that support your side. It can replace Parts C and D of Form 15B, or add to them. Rules 14 (18) and (19) apply to that affidavit. Does the motion ask to change a final support order or a support agreement? Then you must serve and file a financial statement within the same time as your response or consent. Your response (Form 15B) must be served and filed at the same time as the financial statement. This is subject to rule 13 (1.3). Under it, a party making a claim does not have to file a financial statement in one case. That is when their only support claim is for child support in the table amount. That does not apply if there is also a property claim. It also does not apply if there is a claim for exclusive possession (sole use) of the matrimonial home and its contents. The motion may not need a financial statement, but your response may ask to change a support order or support agreement. If so, the financial statement rules apply to you too. With a financial statement, you must serve other papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They include the papers in rule 13 (3.1) and a current list of what is owed from the Family Responsibility Office. If you are the one asking to change or cancel arrears, you must also serve proof of your income for each of those years. This is your income tax return with your notice of assessment, and any notice of reassessment. If those notices are unavailable for a year, use the Canada Revenue Agency's Income and Deductions printout with the return instead. If you do not have to file a tax return and chose not to because of the Indian Act (Canada), serve some other proof of income. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with those papers. File the certificate no later than four days before a case conference. Your response may make a claim about decision-making responsibility or parenting time, net family property, a matrimonial home, or support. If it does, the clerk may give you an automatic order (Form 8.0.1). If the clerk gives you one, you must serve it on every other party. Serve it promptly, and no later than seven days after it is issued.

The full answer for this step, with every rule and source
My ex wants to change our final order — what do I have to do, and by when?

Where things stand

Another party has served you with a motion to change a final order or agreement. The rules give you two ways to reply. Which one you use depends on whether you agree to the change. Your time to reply depends on where you live.

What to do next

Do you disagree with the change, or want the court to make an added or different change? Then you must serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B), with all required attachments. You must do this within 30 days after you get the motion to change and its papers, if you live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, the limit is 60 days. Do you agree to the change, or have you and the other party agreed to a different change? Then you must fill in the parts of the consent motion to change (Form 15C) that apply to you. Within the same 30 or 60 days, you must return a signed copy to the party making the motion. You must also give a copy of the signed consent to the assignee, if there is one. An assignee is an agency or person a support order or agreement has been assigned to. If the order or agreement was assigned, you must serve your response on the assignee as if it were a party. You may use an affidavit to give the facts that support your side. It can replace Parts C and D of Form 15B, or add to them. Rules 14 (18) and (19) apply to that affidavit. Does the motion ask to change a final support order or a support agreement? Then you must serve and file a financial statement within the same time as your response or consent. Your response (Form 15B) must be served and filed at the same time as the financial statement. This is subject to rule 13 (1.3). Under it, a party making a claim does not have to file a financial statement in one case. That is when their only support claim is for child support in the table amount. That does not apply if there is also a property claim. It also does not apply if there is a claim for exclusive possession (sole use) of the matrimonial home and its contents. The motion may not need a financial statement, but your response may ask to change a support order or support agreement. If so, the financial statement rules apply to you too. With a financial statement, you must serve other papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They include the papers in rule 13 (3.1) and a current list of what is owed from the Family Responsibility Office. If you are the one asking to change or cancel arrears, you must also serve proof of your income for each of those years. This is your income tax return with your notice of assessment, and any notice of reassessment. If those notices are unavailable for a year, use the Canada Revenue Agency's Income and Deductions printout with the return instead. If you do not have to file a tax return and chose not to because of the Indian Act (Canada), serve some other proof of income. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with those papers. File the certificate no later than four days before a case conference. Your response may make a claim about decision-making responsibility or parenting time, net family property, a matrimonial home, or support. If it does, the clerk may give you an automatic order (Form 8.0.1). If the clerk gives you one, you must serve it on every other party. Serve it promptly, and no later than seven days after it is issued.

Your deadline

If you do not agree, or want the court to make an added or different change, serve and file a response (Form 15B). If you agree, return a signed consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion. Give a copy to any assignee. You have 30 days after the day you receive the motion to change and its supporting documents. It is 60 days if you do not live in Canada or the United States. The motion may ask to change support, or your response may ask for a support change. If so, your financial statement is due in the same time. Serve the papers the rule lists with it. Examples are the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) and a current schedule of arrears from the Family Responsibility Office. Add a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). Your response may ask for its own change to parenting, property or support. If the clerk then issues an automatic order, serve it promptly, and no later than 7 days after it is issued. Where the information program applies, your certificate must be filed before you serve the response. This is explained below. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take any step in the case except booking a case conference. The rule's other exception is for an answer. It does not mention a response to a motion to change. So where the program applies, attend it and file your certificate before your response is due. Or ask the court on a motion to excuse you. The rule counts the 45 days from when the case started. It says nothing more exact for a motion to change.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

Based on the date you gave us, the last day for this is Monday 2 November 2026.

How that was counted:
- Counted 30 days from Friday 2 October 2026, not counting that day itself and counting the last day, which gives Sunday 1 November 2026.
- Sunday 1 November 2026 is a Sunday, when court offices are closed.
- The period therefore ends on the next day court offices are open: Monday 2 November 2026.

This date was worked out by counting, not taken from your court file. If the date you gave us is not exactly right, this one will not be either — and the court office can confirm both.

What happens after

Say you do not serve and file a response, or return a consent, as required. Then these things apply, unless a court orders otherwise. You do not get notice of more steps in the case, except service of an order. You cannot take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without you, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. The party making the motion may also file a motion form (Form 14B) asking the court to make the order they asked for in their papers. They cannot do this if an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest and opposes the change. If the motion is opposed, a judge must hold at least one conference. Even after you serve and file a response, the parties and any assignee may still agree before the hearing. They may then go ahead on consent by filing the papers rule 15 (19) lists.

O. Reg. 391/97, s. 19 (1); O. Reg. 446/01, s. 6.

The party making the motion may then serve evidence replying to any new matters raised by the evidence served by the party responding to the motion. 4. No other evidence may be used. O. Reg. 114/99, r. 14 (20).

Does the existing support order remain enforceable while the motion is pending, and what rules govern any requested retroactive reduction, cancellation of arrears or temporary change in payment obligations?(1 passage)

Colucci v. Colucci, 2021 SCC 24, para. 7

“Indeed, effective notice in this context is only “effective” when there has been disclosure of the changed financial circumstances.”

A court decision: what the judges said in an earlier case. It has not been checked for later decisions that may have changed it.

Read more of the decision

[7] Given the informational asymmetry between the parties, a payor’s success in obtaining a retroactive decrease will depend largely on the payor’s financial disclosure and communication. Indeed, effective notice in this context is only “effective” when there has been disclosure of the changed financial circumstances. At the stage of considering the D.B.S. factors, disclosure will once again be a key consideration in assessing whether the payor’s conduct operates to shorten or lengthen the presumptive period of retroactivity.

Family Law Rules, O. Reg. 114/99, r. 15 (15)-(16)

Request for order (15) If a party does not serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B) or return a consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion as required under subrule (9), or if the party’s response is struck out by an order, the party making the motion to change may file a motion … Read the whole provision

Request for order (15) If a party does not serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B) or return a consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion as required under subrule (9), or if the party’s response is struck out by an order, the party making the motion to change may file a motion form (Form 14B) asking that the court make the order requested in the materials filed by the party, unless an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest in the motion and opposes the change. O. Reg. 151/08, s. 4; O. Reg. 322/13, s. 9 (2). Consent to motion (16) If a party returns to the party making the motion a consent motion to change (Form 15C) in accordance with subparagraph 2 i of subrule (9), the party making the motion shall complete and file the consent motion to change and, unless any assignee refuses to consent to the change being requested, the party making the motion shall file with the consent motion to change, (a) a motion form (Form 14B) asking that the court make the order described in the consent motion to change; (b) five copies of a draft order; (c) a stamped envelope addressed to each party and to the assignee, if any; and (d) if the order that is agreed on relates in whole or in part to a support obligation, (i) a support deduction order information form prescribed under the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, and (ii) a draft support deduction order. O. Reg. 151/08, s. 4.

Support if family violence is part of your situation
Who to contact, and how

If family violence is part of what you're dealing with, Ontario has support services separate from the court process itself. A Family Court Support Worker can help you understand and go through the family court process if you're a victim of domestic violence -- Family Court Support Workers do not give legal advice, but they can help you understand what's happening and connect you to other services. Every courthouse also has a Family Law Information Centre (FLIC) that provides information about the court process and referrals to local resources.

Ontario also names specific support organizations for family violence:
- Assaulted Women's Helpline: 1-866-863-0511 (toll-free), or 416-863-0511
- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- Victim Support Line: 1-888-579-2888 (toll-free), or 416-314-2447

The Family Court Support Worker Program and the Family Law Information Centre are delivered locally through each court location rather than through a single province-wide phone number. To find the Family Court Support Worker for your court, use Ontario's own listing of service providers by court location, which links directly to the organization delivering the program there. To reach the Family Law Information Centre, contact or visit the courthouse handling your case -- Ontario's own courthouse listing gives the address and contact information, including a phone number, for each location.

Ontario.ca — Violence and Abuse: Family Violence
Ontario.ca — Family Court Support Workers

Ontario.ca — Connect with Supports for Survivors of Violence

Do you disagree with the change, or want the court to make an added or different change? Then you must serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B), with all required attachments. You must do this within 30 days after you get the motion to change and its papers, if you live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, the limit is 60 days. You may use an affidavit to give the facts that support your side. It can replace Parts C and D of Form 15B, or add to them. Rules 14 (18) and (19) apply to that affidavit. If it does, the clerk may give you an automatic order (Form 8.0.1). If the clerk gives you one, you must serve it on every other party. Serve it promptly, and no later than seven days after it is issued.

The full answer for this step, with every rule and source
My ex wants to change our final order — what do I have to do, and by when?

Where things stand

Another party has served you with a motion to change a final order or agreement. The rules give you two ways to reply. Which one you use depends on whether you agree to the change. Your time to reply depends on where you live.

What to do next

Do you disagree with the change, or want the court to make an added or different change? Then you must serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B), with all required attachments. You must do this within 30 days after you get the motion to change and its papers, if you live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, the limit is 60 days. Do you agree to the change, or have you and the other party agreed to a different change? Then you must fill in the parts of the consent motion to change (Form 15C) that apply to you. Within the same 30 or 60 days, you must return a signed copy to the party making the motion. You must also give a copy of the signed consent to the assignee, if there is one. An assignee is an agency or person a support order or agreement has been assigned to. If the order or agreement was assigned, you must serve your response on the assignee as if it were a party. You may use an affidavit to give the facts that support your side. It can replace Parts C and D of Form 15B, or add to them. Rules 14 (18) and (19) apply to that affidavit. Does the motion ask to change a final support order or a support agreement? Then you must serve and file a financial statement within the same time as your response or consent. Your response (Form 15B) must be served and filed at the same time as the financial statement. This is subject to rule 13 (1.3). Under it, a party making a claim does not have to file a financial statement in one case. That is when their only support claim is for child support in the table amount. That does not apply if there is also a property claim. It also does not apply if there is a claim for exclusive possession (sole use) of the matrimonial home and its contents. The motion may not need a financial statement, but your response may ask to change a support order or support agreement. If so, the financial statement rules apply to you too. With a financial statement, you must serve other papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They include the papers in rule 13 (3.1) and a current list of what is owed from the Family Responsibility Office. If you are the one asking to change or cancel arrears, you must also serve proof of your income for each of those years. This is your income tax return with your notice of assessment, and any notice of reassessment. If those notices are unavailable for a year, use the Canada Revenue Agency's Income and Deductions printout with the return instead. If you do not have to file a tax return and chose not to because of the Indian Act (Canada), serve some other proof of income. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with those papers. File the certificate no later than four days before a case conference. Your response may make a claim about decision-making responsibility or parenting time, net family property, a matrimonial home, or support. If it does, the clerk may give you an automatic order (Form 8.0.1). If the clerk gives you one, you must serve it on every other party. Serve it promptly, and no later than seven days after it is issued.

Your deadline

If you do not agree, or want the court to make an added or different change, serve and file a response (Form 15B). If you agree, return a signed consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion. Give a copy to any assignee. You have 30 days after the day you receive the motion to change and its supporting documents. It is 60 days if you do not live in Canada or the United States. The motion may ask to change support, or your response may ask for a support change. If so, your financial statement is due in the same time. Serve the papers the rule lists with it. Examples are the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) and a current schedule of arrears from the Family Responsibility Office. Add a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). Your response may ask for its own change to parenting, property or support. If the clerk then issues an automatic order, serve it promptly, and no later than 7 days after it is issued. Where the information program applies, your certificate must be filed before you serve the response. This is explained below. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take any step in the case except booking a case conference. The rule's other exception is for an answer. It does not mention a response to a motion to change. So where the program applies, attend it and file your certificate before your response is due. Or ask the court on a motion to excuse you. The rule counts the 45 days from when the case started. It says nothing more exact for a motion to change.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

Based on the date you gave us, the last day for this is Monday 2 November 2026.

How that was counted:
- Counted 30 days from Friday 2 October 2026, not counting that day itself and counting the last day, which gives Sunday 1 November 2026.
- Sunday 1 November 2026 is a Sunday, when court offices are closed.
- The period therefore ends on the next day court offices are open: Monday 2 November 2026.

This date was worked out by counting, not taken from your court file. If the date you gave us is not exactly right, this one will not be either — and the court office can confirm both.

What happens after

Say you do not serve and file a response, or return a consent, as required. Then these things apply, unless a court orders otherwise. You do not get notice of more steps in the case, except service of an order. You cannot take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without you, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. The party making the motion may also file a motion form (Form 14B) asking the court to make the order they asked for in their papers. They cannot do this if an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest and opposes the change. If the motion is opposed, a judge must hold at least one conference. Even after you serve and file a response, the parties and any assignee may still agree before the hearing. They may then go ahead on consent by filing the papers rule 15 (19) lists.

These are the questions a careful lawyer would look into for what you described, and what the law in our checked library says about each. The quoted words are from the official text. They say what the law provides, not how your case will turn out.

Which child support legislation and guidelines govern the existing order, and what change in circumstances must the requesting parent establish before the court can reduce support?(4 passages)

Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 17 (2.2)-(4)

“Before the court makes a variation order in respect of a child support order, the court shall satisfy itself that a change of circumstances as provided for in the applicable guidelines has occurred since the making of the child support order or the last variation order made in respect of that order.”
Read more of the provision

Marginal note: Variation of contact order (2.2) If the court makes a variation order in respect of a parenting order, it may make an order varying any contact order to take into account that variation order, and subsections (3) and (11) apply as a consequence with any necessary modifications. Marginal note: Conditions of order (3) The court may include in a variation order any provision that under this Act could have been included in the order in respect of which the variation order is sought, and the court has the same powers and obligations that it would have when making that order. O. Reg. 391/97, s. 19 (1); O. Reg. 446/01, s. 6.

Reg. 114/99, r. 14 (20).

Does the existing support order remain enforceable while the motion is pending, and what rules govern any requested retroactive reduction, cancellation of arrears or temporary change in payment obligations?(1 passage)

Colucci v. Colucci, 2021 SCC 24, para. 7

“Indeed, effective notice in this context is only “effective” when there has been disclosure of the changed financial circumstances.”

A court decision: what the judges said in an earlier case. It has not been checked for later decisions that may have changed it.

Read more of the decision

[7] Given the informational asymmetry between the parties, a payor’s success in obtaining a retroactive decrease will depend largely on the payor’s financial disclosure and communication. Indeed, effective notice in this context is only “effective” when there has been disclosure of the changed financial circumstances. At the stage of considering the D.B.S. factors, disclosure will once again be a key consideration in assessing whether the payor’s conduct operates to shorten or lengthen the presumptive period of retroactivity.

Request for order (15) If a party does not serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B) or return a consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion as required under subrule (9), or if the party’s response is struck out by an order, the party making the motion to change may file a motion form (Form 14B) asking that the court make the order requested in the materials filed by the party, unless an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest in the motion and opposes the change. Consent to motion (16) If a party returns to the party making the motion a consent motion to change (Form 15C) in accordance with subparagraph 2 i of subrule (9), the party making the motion shall complete and file the consent motion to change and, unless any assignee refuses to consent to the change being requested, the party making the motion shall file with the consent motion to change, (a) a motion form (Form 14B) asking that the court make the order described in the consent motion to change; (b) five copies of a draft order; (c) a stamped envelope addressed to each party and to the assignee, if any; and (d) if the order that is agreed on relates in whole or in part to a support obligation, (i) a support deduction order information form prescribed under the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, and (ii) a draft support deduction order. O. Reg. 151/08, s. 4.

Explain in plain wordsOfficial text
Support if family violence is part of your situation
Who to contact, and how

If family violence is part of what you're dealing with, Ontario has support services separate from the court process itself. A Family Court Support Worker can help you understand and go through the family court process if you're a victim of domestic violence -- Family Court Support Workers do not give legal advice, but they can help you understand what's happening and connect you to other services. Every courthouse also has a Family Law Information Centre (FLIC) that provides information about the court process and referrals to local resources.

Ontario also names specific support organizations for family violence:
- Assaulted Women's Helpline: 1-866-863-0511 (toll-free), or 416-863-0511
- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- Victim Support Line: 1-888-579-2888 (toll-free), or 416-314-2447

The Family Court Support Worker Program and the Family Law Information Centre are delivered locally through each court location rather than through a single province-wide phone number. To find the Family Court Support Worker for your court, use Ontario's own listing of service providers by court location, which links directly to the organization delivering the program there. To reach the Family Law Information Centre, contact or visit the courthouse handling your case -- Ontario's own courthouse listing gives the address and contact information, including a phone number, for each location.

Ontario.ca — Connect with Supports for Survivors of Violence

WHAT THE STATUTES SAY ABOUT WHICH COURT

Which court hears a family case depends on what is being asked for. The Divorce Act defines "court", for Ontario, as the Superior Court of Justice — so a divorce, and any parenting, contact or support order asked for as part of a divorce, is not heard in the Ontario Court of Justice.

Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 2 (1)

The Family Law Act's property rules (Part I) and matrimonial home rules (Part II) each define "court" to exclude the Ontario Court of Justice. Support and parenting under the Ontario statutes may be heard in the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court, or the Superior Court of Justice.

Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3, ss. 1 (1), 4 (1), 17

In 24 named municipalities there is a single Family Court that hears all of it. Proceedings listed in the Courts of Justice Act's Schedule "shall be commenced, heard and determined in the Family Court" there. A case may be started in the Family Court if either party lives in one of those municipalities.

Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, ss. 21.8 (1), 21.11 (1)
O. Reg. 114/99 (Family Law Rules), r. 1 (3)

This produces your application and the rule that decides the amount. It does not calculate the amount. The figure comes from a table that takes an income defined by O. Reg. 391/97 s. 16 and adjusted by Schedule III, and ss. 17 to 20 let a court determine that income differently again. Nothing on this site works out what you would receive or owe.

QUESTION 1

Who is applying, and who is the application against?

QUESTION 2

Where does the other parent ordinarily live?

This decides which table applies, so it is worth getting right. O. Reg. 391/97 s. 2 (1) selects the table for the province or territory where the parent the order is sought againstordinarily resides — not where the children live and not where the case is filed. If they live elsewhere in Canada, that province’s or territory’s table applies. If they live outside Canada, or you do not know where they live, the Ontario table applies when you live in Ontario (s. 2 (1), “table”, (b) and (e)).

QUESTION 3

Tell me about the children this is for.

Each child’s age, and what each is doing now — at school, working, or something else. In your own words; this goes into the application as you write it.

QUESTION 4

How is the children’s time divided between you at the moment?

Recorded as you describe it. Whether O. Reg. 391/97 s. 8 or s. 9 applies to an arrangement is for the court; nothing here decides that.

QUESTION 5

What is the other parent’s annual income, and where does that figure come from?

Write it however you know it. If you are unsure, say so in your own words — “about $60,000” is recorded as you wrote it and is not rounded or changed.

We have both agreed on this figure, in writing.
O. Reg. 391/97 s. 15 (2) provides that where both parties agree in writing on the annual income of a party, the court may consider that amount to be their income if it thinks the amount is reasonable having regard to the income information provided under s. 21. A figure agreed in writing and a figure one person states are read differently, so the application says which this is.
When a court works out the income figure itself
s. 17 — Where the court is of the opinion that s. 16 would not be the fairest determination, it may have regard to income over the last three years and determine an amount that is fair and reasonable in light of any pattern, fluctuation, or non-recurring amount.
s. 18 — Where a person is a shareholder, director or officer of a corporation and the court is of the opinion that s. 16 does not fairly reflect all the money available for support, the court may include corporate pre-tax income or an amount commensurate with services provided.
s. 19 — The court may impute income in circumstances the section lists, including intentional under-employment or unemployment, diverted income, property not reasonably used to generate income, failure to provide income information when legally obliged to, and unreasonably deducted expenses.
s. 20 — Where a person is a non-resident, income is generally determined as though they were a resident of Canada, with a different rule where they reside where effective tax rates are significantly higher.
Schedule III, item 9 — Salaries, benefits, wages or management fees paid to non-arm's-length persons and deducted from net self-employment income are added back UNLESS the person establishes the payments were necessary to earn the income and reasonable in the circumstances. That is something a person must establish, not something to be calculated.
Schedule III, item 12 — Where income is earned through a partnership or sole proprietorship, an amount included in income that is "properly required" by the business for capitalization is deducted. Whether an amount is properly required is a judgment, not arithmetic.

QUESTION 6

Is this only about the table amount for the children?

If it is — no spousal support, no share of special expenses, nothing about property — Family Law Rules r. 13 (1.3) means you do not have to file a financial statement at all. That is a whole form you would otherwise complete.

Yes, only the table amount
No, there is more to it

QUESTION 7

Which income documents do you already have? One per line.

Under O. Reg. 391/97 s. 21 (1), a parent applying for child support whose income information is necessary to determine the amount must include with the application their income tax returns and notices of assessment for the three most recent taxation years, and the other documents the section lists. The parent served with the application must provide the same documents, if their income information is necessary, within 30 days after being served (60 days if they live outside Canada and the United States) (s. 21 (2)). Listing none is a real answer — the application says so rather than leaving a blank.

HOW THE TABLE WORKS

How a table amount is worked out: find the income row, then add the percentage

This explains how the table is built. It is not about your case, and no amount is worked out here or anywhere else on this site.

Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (1)

Unless otherwise provided under these guidelines, the amount of an order for the support of a child for children under the age of majority is,

(a) the amount set out in the applicable table, according to the number of children under the age of majority to whom the order relates and the income of the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought; and

(b) the amount, if any, determined under section 7.

Two parts, and only the first comes from the table. Section 7 covers special or extraordinary expenses, and the court decides those separately.

Which table — it depends on where the other parent lives

Ontario does not publish a table of its own. O. Reg. 303/24 revoked the one it had, and s. 2 (1) of the Ontario Guidelines now defines “table” by pointing at the federal tables:

“table” means,

(a) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides in Ontario at the time of the application, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for Ontario,

(b) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides elsewhere in Canada, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for the province or territory in which the parent or spouse ordinarily resides at the time of the application …

It is where the person the order is sought againstordinarily resides — not where the case is filed and not where the child lives. Your own residence matters only if that person lives outside Canada or where they live is unknown: then the Ontario table applies when you live in Ontario (paragraph (e)). Paragraphs (c) and (d) go further: a court may use a different province’s table where that residence has changed since the application, or will change in the near future.

What a table looks like

Each table is headed by a province and a number of children, and carries two tiers of columns. The columns below are shown empty on purpose — the figures are at the source.

Income ($)	Monthly Award ($)
From	To	Basic Amount	Plus (%)	Of Income Over
—	—	—	—	—

A row’s award is not the Basic Amount on its own. It is the Basic Amount plusthe percentage in Plus (%) applied to the income above the “Of Income Over” figure, which is the floor of that row’s band. That is what makes a row a calculation rather than an answer.

The income the table takes is a defined figure

It is not a salary and not a take-home figure. O. Reg. 391/97 s. 16 determines annual income using the sources listed under “Total income” in the T1 General form, adjusted in accordance with Schedule III. Sections 17 to 20 set out circumstances in which a court determines the figure differently again — a pattern of income over three years, income from a corporation, or an amount imputed to a parent or spouse.

That is why this site records what you tell it about income and does not turn it into a support amount. The figure the table takes is one a court determines.

Sources, read in full at: O. Reg. 391/97 (Ontario) · SOR/97-175 (federal) · the federal tables themselves. Verified 2026-09-15.

We have both agreed on this figure, in writing.

A figure agreed in writing and a figure one person states are read differently, so the application says which this is.
When a court works out the income figure itself
s. 17 — Where the court is of the opinion that s. 16 would not be the fairest determination, it may have regard to income over the last three years and determine an amount that is fair and reasonable in light of any pattern, fluctuation, or non-recurring amount.
s. 18 — Where a person is a shareholder, director or officer of a corporation and the court is of the opinion that s. 16 does not fairly reflect all the money available for support, the court may include corporate pre-tax income or an amount commensurate with services provided.
s. 19 — The court may impute income in circumstances the section lists, including intentional under-employment or unemployment, diverted income, property not reasonably used to generate income, failure to provide income information when legally obliged to, and unreasonably deducted expenses.
s. 20 — Where a person is a non-resident, income is generally determined as though they were a resident of Canada, with a different rule where they reside where effective tax rates are significantly higher.
Schedule III, item 9 — Salaries, benefits, wages or management fees paid to non-arm's-length persons and deducted from net self-employment income are added back UNLESS the person establishes the payments were necessary to earn the income and reasonable in the circumstances. That is something a person must establish, not something to be calculated.
Schedule III, item 12 — Where income is earned through a partnership or sole proprietorship, an amount included in income that is "properly required" by the business for capitalization is deducted. Whether an amount is properly required is a judgment, not arithmetic.

HOW THE TABLE WORKS

How a table amount is worked out: find the income row, then add the percentage

This explains how the table is built. It is not about your case, and no amount is worked out here or anywhere else on this site.

Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (1)

Unless otherwise provided under these guidelines, the amount of an order for the support of a child for children under the age of majority is,

(a) the amount set out in the applicable table, according to the number of children under the age of majority to whom the order relates and the income of the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought; and

(b) the amount, if any, determined under section 7.

Two parts, and only the first comes from the table. Section 7 covers special or extraordinary expenses, and the court decides those separately.

Which table — it depends on where the other parent lives

Ontario does not publish a table of its own. O. Reg. 303/24 revoked the one it had, and s. 2 (1) of the Ontario Guidelines now defines “table” by pointing at the federal tables:

“table” means,

(a) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides in Ontario at the time of the application, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for Ontario,

(b) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides elsewhere in Canada, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for the province or territory in which the parent or spouse ordinarily resides at the time of the application …

It is where the person the order is sought againstordinarily resides — not where the case is filed and not where the child lives. Your own residence matters only if that person lives outside Canada or where they live is unknown: then the Ontario table applies when you live in Ontario (paragraph (e)). Paragraphs (c) and (d) go further: a court may use a different province’s table where that residence has changed since the application, or will change in the near future.

What a table looks like

Each table is headed by a province and a number of children, and carries two tiers of columns. The columns below are shown empty on purpose — the figures are at the source.

Income ($)	Monthly Award ($)
From	To	Basic Amount	Plus (%)	Of Income Over
—	—	—	—	—

A row’s award is not the Basic Amount on its own. It is the Basic Amount plusthe percentage in Plus (%) applied to the income above the “Of Income Over” figure, which is the floor of that row’s band. That is what makes a row a calculation rather than an answer.

The income the table takes is a defined figure

It is not a salary and not a take-home figure. O. Reg. 391/97 s. 16 determines annual income using the sources listed under “Total income” in the T1 General form, adjusted in accordance with Schedule III. Sections 17 to 20 set out circumstances in which a court determines the figure differently again — a pattern of income over three years, income from a corporation, or an amount imputed to a parent or spouse.

That is why this site records what you tell it about income and does not turn it into a support amount. The figure the table takes is one a court determines.

WHAT THE STATUTES SAY ABOUT WHICH COURT

Which court hears a family case depends on what is being asked for. The Divorce Act defines "court", for Ontario, as the Superior Court of Justice — so a divorce, and any parenting, contact or support order asked for as part of a divorce, is not heard in the Ontario Court of Justice.

Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 2 (1)

The Family Law Act's property rules (Part I) and matrimonial home rules (Part II) each define "court" to exclude the Ontario Court of Justice. Support and parenting under the Ontario statutes may be heard in the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court, or the Superior Court of Justice.

Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3, ss. 1 (1), 4 (1), 17

In 24 named municipalities there is a single Family Court that hears all of it. Proceedings listed in the Courts of Justice Act's Schedule "shall be commenced, heard and determined in the Family Court" there. A case may be started in the Family Court if either party lives in one of those municipalities.

Your step: There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it? Not right? Choose another step

YOUR NEXT STEP

Where you are: Support or other order not being obeyed

While a support order is filed there, only the Director may enforce it. The one exception is someone given the Director's powers under section 4 of the Act. The Director may refuse to enforce all or part of a filed order in some cases the Act lists. They include an order whose meaning is unclear. They also include when the person owed support has not met reasonable requests for facts the Director needs. An order that was withdrawn from the Director's office may be filed there again at any time. The payor or the recipient does this by signing a written notice. A support order and any support deduction order that goes with it must be filed again together. Whoever files or refiles a support order there must give notice right away. It goes to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order. It can be sent by mail or email. It can also be sent online, through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. A person owed support who files the order there may have started to enforce it on their own. If the Director asks, they must hand that over to the Director. A payment order is a temporary or final order to pay money to another person, such as a support order. It does not include a provisional order. The Family Law Rules list ways to enforce a payment order. Who uses these ways depends on where the order is. While a support order is filed in the Director's office, only the Director may use them, apart from the exception above. If it is not filed there, the person owed the money may. The ways include a request for a financial statement, seizure and sale, and garnishment. A default hearing can also be used if the order is a support order. When the Director enforces an order, the rules for the person the order favours apply to the Director. Other orders may be enforced in three ways. They are a writ to seize property for a time, a contempt order, and naming a receiver. All of these are in addition to other ways the law provides.

Sources: Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 31, s. 2; Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 31, s. 5 (1); Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 31, s. 12 (1); Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 31, s. 6 (7) — all sources are in the full answer below.

The full answer for this step, with every rule and source
There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it?

Where things stand

Ontario has a Director of the Family Responsibility Office. The Director's job is to enforce support orders filed in the Director's office. This applies when the order, and any support deduction order that goes with it, are filed there. The Director pays what is collected to the person it is owed to. The clerk or registrar of the court that made a support order must file it there promptly once it is signed.

What to do next

While a support order is filed there, only the Director may enforce it. The one exception is someone given the Director's powers under section 4 of the Act. The Director may refuse to enforce all or part of a filed order in some cases the Act lists. They include an order whose meaning is unclear. They also include when the person owed support has not met reasonable requests for facts the Director needs. An order that was withdrawn from the Director's office may be filed there again at any time. The payor or the recipient does this by signing a written notice. A support order and any support deduction order that goes with it must be filed again together. Whoever files or refiles a support order there must give notice right away. It goes to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order. It can be sent by mail or email. It can also be sent online, through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. A person owed support who files the order there may have started to enforce it on their own. If the Director asks, they must hand that over to the Director. A payment order is a temporary or final order to pay money to another person, such as a support order. It does not include a provisional order. The Family Law Rules list ways to enforce a payment order. Who uses these ways depends on where the order is. While a support order is filed in the Director's office, only the Director may use them, apart from the exception above. If it is not filed there, the person owed the money may. The ways include a request for a financial statement, seizure and sale, and garnishment. A default hearing can also be used if the order is a support order. When the Director enforces an order, the rules for the person the order favours apply to the Director. Other orders may be enforced in three ways. They are a writ to seize property for a time, a contempt order, and naming a receiver. All of these are in addition to other ways the law provides.

What happens after

Using one way to enforce a support order does not stop other ways at the same time or at other times. The Director may enforce arrears that built up before the order was filed there. If an order is withdrawn, the Director must stop enforcing it. But the Director may keep enforcing to collect arrears owed to an agency from a past assignment.

What enforcement duties and powers does the Family Responsibility Office have for an unpaid child support order, and how can the recipient request an enforcement review or escalate concerns about inactivity?(1 passage)

Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 31, s. 5 (1)-(3)

“5 (1) It is the duty of the Director to enforce support orders where the support order and the related support deduction order, if any, are filed in the Director’s office and to pay the amounts collected to the person to whom they are owed.”
Read more of the provision

5 (1) It is the duty of the Director to enforce support orders where the support order and the related support deduction order, if any, are filed in the Director’s office and to pay the amounts collected to the person to whom they are owed. 1996, c. 31, s. 5 (1). Transition (2) Subject to subsection (4), a support order or support deduction order that is filed in the office of the Director of the Family Support Plan immediately before the day this section comes into force shall be deemed to be filed in the Director’s office on the day this section comes into force. 1996, c. 31, s. 5 (2). Same (3) If a support deduction order is filed in the office of the Director of the Family Support Plan immediately before the day this section comes into force and the related support order was never filed in his or her office before that day, it is the duty of the Director to enforce the support deduction order so long as it is filed in the Director’s office. 1996, c. 31, s. 5 (3).

Explain in plain wordsOfficial text
While the order is filed with the Family Responsibility Office, may the recipient enforce it independently, what permission or withdrawal process is required, and which court has jurisdiction?(2 passages)

Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 31, s. 16 (1)-(3)

“16 (1) A support order or support deduction order filed in the office of the Director may be withdrawn at any time, as described in subsection (1.1), unless the support order states that it and the related support deduction order cannot be withdrawn from the Director’s office.”
Read more of the provision

16 (1) A support order or support deduction order filed in the office of the Director may be withdrawn at any time, as described in subsection (1.1), unless the support order states that it and the related support deduction order cannot be withdrawn from the Director’s office. 2005, c. 16, s. 6. Method (1.1) Withdrawal is effected by a written notice signed by, (a) the recipient and the payor, if the payor is in compliance as defined in the regulations; or (b) the recipient, if the payor is not in compliance as defined in the regulations. 2005, c. 16, s. 6. Consent of agency filing order (2) A support order and related support deduction order, if any, that have been assigned to an agency referred to in subsection 14 (1) may not be withdrawn under subsection (1) except by the agency or with the consent of the agency so long as the orders are under assignment. 1997, c. 25, Sched. E, s. 2 (3). Effect of withdrawal (3) The Director shall cease enforcement of an order upon its withdrawal from the Director’s office. 1996, c. 31, s. 16 (3).

Explain in plain wordsOfficial text

Family Law Rules, O. Reg. 114/99, r. 5 (4)-(6)

“All steps in enforcement of a payment order, including a motion to suspend a support deduction order, shall take place, (a) in the municipality where the recipient resides; (b) if the recipient does not reside in Ontario, in the municipality where the order is filed with the court for enforcement; (c) if the person enforcing the order so chooses, in the municipality where the payor resides;”

Place for steps other than enforcement (4) All steps in the case, other than enforcement, shall take place in the municipality where the case is started or transferred. O. Reg. 114/99, r. 5 (4). Exception: special provisions (2.3) Despite subsection (2.2), a court may award an amount that is different from the amount that would be determined in accordance with the child support guidelines if the court is satisfied, (a) that special provisions in an order or a written agreement respecting the financial obligations of the parents, or the division or transfer of their property, directly or indirectly benefit a child, or that special provisions have otherwise been made for the benefit of a child; and (b) that the application of the child support guidelines would result in an amount of child support that is inequitable given those special provisions. 1997, c. 20, s. 6.

Support if family violence is part of your situation
Who to contact, and how

If family violence is part of what you're dealing with, Ontario has support services separate from the court process itself. A Family Court Support Worker can help you understand and go through the family court process if you're a victim of domestic violence -- Family Court Support Workers do not give legal advice, but they can help you understand what's happening and connect you to other services. Every courthouse also has a Family Law Information Centre (FLIC) that provides information about the court process and referrals to local resources.

Ontario also names specific support organizations for family violence:
- Assaulted Women's Helpline: 1-866-863-0511 (toll-free), or 416-863-0511
- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- Victim Support Line: 1-888-579-2888 (toll-free), or 416-314-2447

The Family Court Support Worker Program and the Family Law Information Centre are delivered locally through each court location rather than through a single province-wide phone number. To find the Family Court Support Worker for your court, use Ontario's own listing of service providers by court location, which links directly to the organization delivering the program there. To reach the Family Law Information Centre, contact or visit the courthouse handling your case -- Ontario's own courthouse listing gives the address and contact information, including a phone number, for each location.

WHAT THE STATUTES SAY ABOUT WHICH COURT

Which court hears a family case depends on what is being asked for. The Divorce Act defines "court", for Ontario, as the Superior Court of Justice — so a divorce, and any parenting, contact or support order asked for as part of a divorce, is not heard in the Ontario Court of Justice.

Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 2 (1)

The Family Law Act's property rules (Part I) and matrimonial home rules (Part II) each define "court" to exclude the Ontario Court of Justice. Support and parenting under the Ontario statutes may be heard in the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court, or the Superior Court of Justice.

Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3, ss. 1 (1), 4 (1), 17

In 24 named municipalities there is a single Family Court that hears all of it. Proceedings listed in the Courts of Justice Act's Schedule "shall be commenced, heard and determined in the Family Court" there. A case may be started in the Family Court if either party lives in one of those municipalities.

Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, ss. 21.8 (1), 21.11 (1)
O. Reg. 114/99 (Family Law Rules), r. 1 (3)

When a court works out the income figure itself
s. 17 — Where the court is of the opinion that s. 16 would not be the fairest determination, it may have regard to income over the last three years and determine an amount that is fair and reasonable in light of any pattern, fluctuation, or non-recurring amount.
s. 18 — Where a person is a shareholder, director or officer of a corporation and the court is of the opinion that s. 16 does not fairly reflect all the money available for support, the court may include corporate pre-tax income or an amount commensurate with services provided.
s. 19 — The court may impute income in circumstances the section lists, including intentional under-employment or unemployment, diverted income, property not reasonably used to generate income, failure to provide income information when legally obliged to, and unreasonably deducted expenses.
s. 20 — Where a person is a non-resident, income is generally determined as though they were a resident of Canada, with a different rule where they reside where effective tax rates are significantly higher.
Schedule III, item 9 — Salaries, benefits, wages or management fees paid to non-arm's-length persons and deducted from net self-employment income are added back UNLESS the person establishes the payments were necessary to earn the income and reasonable in the circumstances. That is something a person must establish, not something to be calculated.
Schedule III, item 12 — Where income is earned through a partnership or sole proprietorship, an amount included in income that is "properly required" by the business for capitalization is deducted. Whether an amount is properly required is a judgment, not arithmetic.

HOW THE TABLE WORKS

How a table amount is worked out: find the income row, then add the percentage

This explains how the table is built. It is not about your case, and no amount is worked out here or anywhere else on this site.

Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (1)

Unless otherwise provided under these guidelines, the amount of an order for the support of a child for children under the age of majority is,

(a) the amount set out in the applicable table, according to the number of children under the age of majority to whom the order relates and the income of the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought; and

(b) the amount, if any, determined under section 7.

Two parts, and only the first comes from the table. Section 7 covers special or extraordinary expenses, and the court decides those separately.

Which table — it depends on where the other parent lives

Ontario does not publish a table of its own. O. Reg. 303/24 revoked the one it had, and s. 2 (1) of the Ontario Guidelines now defines “table” by pointing at the federal tables:

“table” means,

(a) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides in Ontario at the time of the application, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for Ontario,

(b) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides elsewhere in Canada, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for the province or territory in which the parent or spouse ordinarily resides at the time of the application …

It is where the person the order is sought againstordinarily resides — not where the case is filed and not where the child lives. Your own residence matters only if that person lives outside Canada or where they live is unknown: then the Ontario table applies when you live in Ontario (paragraph (e)). Paragraphs (c) and (d) go further: a court may use a different province’s table where that residence has changed since the application, or will change in the near future.

What a table looks like

Each table is headed by a province and a number of children, and carries two tiers of columns. The columns below are shown empty on purpose — the figures are at the source.

Income ($)	Monthly Award ($)
From	To	Basic Amount	Plus (%)	Of Income Over
—	—	—	—	—

A row’s award is not the Basic Amount on its own. It is the Basic Amount plusthe percentage in Plus (%) applied to the income above the “Of Income Over” figure, which is the floor of that row’s band. That is what makes a row a calculation rather than an answer.

The income the table takes is a defined figure

It is not a salary and not a take-home figure. O. Reg. 391/97 s. 16 determines annual income using the sources listed under “Total income” in the T1 General form, adjusted in accordance with Schedule III. Sections 17 to 20 set out circumstances in which a court determines the figure differently again — a pattern of income over three years, income from a corporation, or an amount imputed to a parent or spouse.

That is why this site records what you tell it about income and does not turn it into a support amount. The figure the table takes is one a court determines.

Sources, read in full at: O. Reg. 391/97 (Ontario) · SOR/97-175 (federal) · the federal tables themselves. Verified 2026-09-15.

WHAT THE STATUTES SAY ABOUT WHICH COURT

Which court hears a family case depends on what is being asked for. The Divorce Act defines "court", for Ontario, as the Superior Court of Justice — so a divorce, and any parenting, contact or support order asked for as part of a divorce, is not heard in the Ontario Court of Justice.

Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 2 (1)

The Family Law Act's property rules (Part I) and matrimonial home rules (Part II) each define "court" to exclude the Ontario Court of Justice. Support and parenting under the Ontario statutes may be heard in the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court, or the Superior Court of Justice.

Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3, ss. 1 (1), 4 (1), 17

In 24 named municipalities there is a single Family Court that hears all of it. Proceedings listed in the Courts of Justice Act's Schedule "shall be commenced, heard and determined in the Family Court" there. A case may be started in the Family Court if either party lives in one of those municipalities.
